newsitem.title: USA: United Air, flight attendants reach pact.
newsitem.headline: United Air, flight attendants reach pact.

text.p: Flight attendants at UAL Corp's United Airlines said Monday they reached a tentative contract pact with the nation's largest airline.
The union declined to provide specific terms of the tentative agreement "but we did meet our primary goals of getting raises, retirement and respect," said Jill Gallagher, a union spokeswoman.
The agreement must still be approved by the union's 22,000 flight attendant members.
Representative from United could not be immediately reached for comment.
Negotiators for the Association of Flight Attendants AFL-CIO reached the tentative agreement with United Airlines negotiators on July 12 after a marathon 25-hour final bargaining session.
The flight attendants union and the airline have been in talks since the current contract became amendable in March 1996.

Talks between the flight attendants and the airline were, at time, contentious, the union said. During negotiations, the flight attendants picketed as part of its "CHAOS" campaign to "Create Havoc Around Our System."

"The talks were very contentious. But that's not unusual in contract negotiations. But I would anticipate that whatever problems we had will be left at the bargaining table and everyone will get back to work," said AFA International President Pat Friend.
The agreement with the flight attendants follow's United recent contract pacts with the pilots and machinists unions.
The flight attendants said those recent agreements "have an impact, obviously, on negotiations. It's clearly something that plays a role," Friend said.
Friend declined to comment specifically on how the flight attendants' agreement compares to those reached with the machinists and pilots, but she said "the committee feels that they are comparable."

The pilots' recent agreement calls for two mid-term wage increases of five percent. In the year 2000, the pact also restores wage rates to levels that existed before July 1994, when certain United employees agreed to wage reduction in exchange for an ownership stake in the company.
The flight attendants, however, did not take part of the 1994 employee stock ownership plan (ESOP).
